A [[set function]] is called '''fractionally subadditive''', or '''XOS''' (not to be confused with [[Assignment valuation|OXS]]), if it is the maximum of several non-negative [[additive set function]]s.
This valuation class was defined, and termed XOS, by [[Noam Nisan]], in the context of [[combinatorial auction]]s.<ref name=n00>{{cite conference|doi=10.1145/352871.352872|chapter=Bidding and allocation in combinatorial auctions|title=Proceedings of the 2nd ACM conference on Electronic commerce - EC '00|page=1|year=2000|last1=Nisan|first1=Noam|isbn=1-58113-272-7}}</ref> The term fractionally subadditive was given by [[Uriel Feige]].<ref name=f09>{{cite journal|doi=10.1137/070680977|title=On Maximizing Welfare when Utility Functions Are Subadditive|journal=SIAM Journal on Computing|volume=39|pages=122–142|year=2009|last1=Feige|first1=Uriel}}</ref>

== Definition ==
There is a finite base set of items, <math>M := \{1,\ldots,m\}</math>.

There is a function <math>v</math> which assigns a number to each subset of <math>M</math>.

The function  <math>v</math> is called ''fractionally subadditive'' (or XOS) if there exists a collection of set functions, <math>\{a_1,\ldots,a_l\}</math>, such that:<ref name=cks16>{{cite journal|doi=10.1145/2835172|title=Bayesian Combinatorial Auctions|journal=Journal of the ACM|volume=63|issue=2|page=1|year=2016|last1=Christodoulou|first1=George|last2=Kovács|first2=Annamária|last3=Schapira|first3=Michael}}</ref>
* Each <math>a_j</math> is additive, ''i.e.'', it assigns to each subset <math>X\subseteq M</math>, the sum of the values of  the items in <math>X</math>.
* The function <math>v</math> is the [[pointwise maximum]] of the functions <math>a_j</math>. I.e, for every subset <math>X\subseteq M</math>:
:<math>v(X) = \max_{j=1}^l a_j(X)</math>

=== Equivalent Definition ===

The name fractionally subadditive comes from the following equivalent definition when restricted to non-negative additive functions: a set function <math> v </math> is ''fractionally subadditive'' if, for any <math> S\subseteq M</math> and any collection <math> \{\alpha_i, T_i\}_{i=1}^k</math> with <math>\alpha_i > 0</math> and <math>T_i\subseteq M</math> such that <math> \sum_{T_i \ni j} \alpha_i \ge 1</math> for all <math>j\in S</math>, we have <math> v(S) \le \sum_{i=1}^k \alpha_i v(T_i) </math>.

== Relation to other utility functions ==
Every [[submodular set function]] is XOS, and every XOS function is a [[subadditive set function]].<ref name=n00/>

See also: [[Utility functions on indivisible goods]].

== Etymology ==
The term XOS stands for '''X'''OR-of-'''O'''Rs of '''S'''ingleton valuations.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lehmann |first1=Benny |last2=Lehmann |first2=Daniel |last3=Nisan |first3=Noam |chapter=Combinatorial auctions with decreasing marginal utilities |date=2001-10-14 |title=Proceedings of the 3rd ACM conference on Electronic Commerce |chapter-url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/501158.501161 |series=EC '01 |location=New York, NY, USA |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |pages=18–28 |doi=10.1145/501158.501161 |isbn=978-1-58113-387-5|arxiv=cs/0202015 }}</ref> 

A Singleton valuation is a valuation function <math>v(\cdot)</math> such that there exists a value <math>w</math> and item <math>i</math> such that <math>v(S):=w</math> if and only if <math>i \in S</math>, and <math>v(S):=0</math> otherwise. That is, a Singleton valuation has value <math>w</math> for receiving item <math>i</math> and has no value for any other items.

An OR of valuations <math>\{v_1(\cdot),v_2(\cdot),\ldots,v_k(\cdot)\}</math> interprets each <math>v_j(\cdot)</math> as representing a distinct player. The OR of <math>\{v_1(\cdot),v_2(\cdot),\ldots,v_k(\cdot)\}</math> is a valuation function <math>v(\cdot)</math> such that <math>v(S):=\max_{S_1,\ldots, S_k\text{ s.th. }S_j\cap S_\ell = \emptyset\ \forall j,\ell\text{ and } \cup_j S_j = S} \{\sum_{j=1}^k v_j(S_j)\}</math>. That is, the OR of valuations <math>\{v_1(\cdot),v_2(\cdot),\ldots,v_k(\cdot)\}</math> is the optimal welfare that can be achieved by partitioning <math>S</math> among players with valuations <math>\{v_1(\cdot),v_2(\cdot),\ldots,v_k(\cdot)\}</math>. The term "OR" refers to the fact that any of the players <math>\{v_1(\cdot),v_2(\cdot),\ldots,v_k(\cdot)\}</math> can receive items. Observe that an OR of Singleton valuations is an additive function.

An XOR of valuations <math>\{v_1(\cdot),\ldots, v_k(\cdot)\}</math> is a valuation function <math>v(\cdot)</math> such that <math>v(S):=\max_{j} \{v_j(S)\}</math>. The term "XOR" refers to the fact that exactly one (an "[[exclusive or]]") of the players can receive items. Observe that an XOR of additive functions is XOS.
